READING PASSAGE 2

You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14-26, which are based on Reading
Passage 2 on pages 6 and 7.

Mimicry and parenting
Becoming our own parents in child-rearing

A Inmany countries today children are primarily brought up by their mothers
and fathers, which means that parents have a considerable effect on the kind
of parenting style their children will adopt in the future. Dr Jerrold Shapiro, a
licensed clinical psychologist, said that realizing that in parenting we behave
just as our parents did is a common experience. For some people this
recognition of our parents within ourselves can be comforting, but for others it
is discouraging. ‘Even if you had good parents,’ adds Shapiro, ‘children are
familiar with their parents’ faults and set out to be different. And yet, we all
have that moment of recognition where we still find our parents within us.’

B But why can't we ever escape the maternal grasp? The answer is that our
imitation of our parents is a response that is deeply embedded in our brains.
Dr Stephanie Cacioppo, Assistant Professor at the Department of Psychiatry
and Behavioral Neuroscience at The University of Chicago, studies what
happens in the brain when we experience love. As she explains, ‘Love creates
chemical substances such as dopamine that activate brain areas involved in
these complex functions: emotion, reward, goal-directed behavior, decision-
making. These happen on various levels in the brain.’ In other words, when
we love, it influences how our brain acts, thinks and responds, and no matter
how you feel about your parents now, as a child, they are your first love.

C The regions of our brain that are activated by our love responses are also
involved in our abstract definition of self. Cacioppo notes that this has led to
speculation that the people we love and who love us back are integral to our
representations of ourselves. Her research has also found that when we love,
the very neurons in our brain begin to mimic those of the person that we are
involved with. ‘The more a woman identifies with her mother (or sees herself
in her mother),’ Cacioppo adds, ‘the more a similar self-expansion (and self-
integration) process occurs. We identified overlapping brain areas for such
simulation process and love, which could explain why this matching process
tends to occur in love, including maternal love.’

D The copying process starts at a very early age. Dr Susan Jones, Professor of
Psychological and Brain Sciences at Indiana University, studies mimicry in
infants, specifically, how infants and their parents imitate one another. She

copying the movements of others. Mimicry starts to pay off in this way quite

D The copying process starts at a very early age. Dr Susan Jones, Professor of

early; for example, children around two years of age begin to engage in
pretend play that includes mimicry of actions like talking on the phone,

pages.text:
driving, Sweeping up or cooking at the stove, using motions that they’ve seen
others do. Language acquisition also involves mimicry, copying the sounds
that make words and the tones in the sentences. And of course, the language,
socially normative behaviors and practical skills that young children learn
through observation and reproduce as mimicry do stay with them as they
grow older.’

We don't just mimic our parents. Jones says that we unconsciously mimic the
people we admire, like our friends or dates. She believes that caregivers who
imitate their babies contribute to the development of the ability to mimic, and
they do this by putting their version of the movement or behavior right next to
the infant’s version. Consequently, as Jones points out, ‘The infant can begin
to associate a body part and its movement that feels like this, with a body
part and movement that looks like that. In other words, caregivers’ imitation
of infants might help infants to map their own bodies and movements onto
the bodies and movements of others.’

Dr Ann Bigelow, a Professor and Researcher of Developmental Psychology at
St Francis Xavier University, has done extensive research on the first contact
between mother and child, and found similar results — our sense of self comes
through our deeply engrained mimicry of others. Specifically, Bigelow has
studied skin-to-skin contact between mother and newborn right after birth.
She explains that this contact helps the newborn ‘adjust from the prenatal to
the postnatal life’. Bigelow adds that while no one is exactly sure why the
skin-to-skin contact is so powerful, she does note that the mother and child's
bodies are so in-tune that, for example, if the baby’s temperature drops, the
mother’s will elevate. Bigelow further explains that when a mother is reacting
and imitating her baby, the baby learns sooner that its actions impact the
world around it. So a baby who has skin-to-skin contact often and early in its
life has a better connection to the mother, and is better able to learn from her.

In sum, much like Jones’s research on mimicry, Bigelow’s research shows that
in order to become ourselves, we must first imitate. And the person we first
learn to imitate is our mother. As Shapiro explains, she is the person who is
there from the moment we are born, and we experience the world through
her. Also, while in some parts of the world children may be raised in multi-
generational households, the Western model of child-rearing is insular. ‘We
live in homes that are defined by a small nuclear family,’ Shapiro says. “There
aren't a lot of alternative models, especially in early childhood.’ Our parents
are for the longest time our only model of adulthood.
